title: Quantifying Climate Disequilibrium and Committed Retreat of Greenland’s Peripheral Glaciers Using Landsat-Derived Accumulation Area Ratios
text:
1 Methods

1.1 Model Training and Validation
Machine learning (ML) classification of Landsat images was based on a modified version of methods published by Aberle et al. (2025). Initial training data in the form of manually labeled glacier surface cover points and corresponding Landsat images were acquired courtesy of Aberle et al. for 4 USGS Benchmark glaciers (Gulkana, South Cascade, Sperry, and Wolverine) across 7 Landsat images, for a total of 8,162 training points. These labeled training points were augmented with an additional 2,650 training points within Greenland, for a combined total of 10,812 training points. For Greenland training data, two locations were chosen, Mittivakkat glacier in the south east, and a heavily glaciated rocky peninsula in the central west (72°N, 54°W; north of Disko Island). Additionally, the “cloud” class was added to the list of 5 landcover types from Aberle et al. (2025), bringing the total number of land cover classifications to 6, “cloud”, “ice/firn”, “rock”, “shadowed snow”, “snow”, and “water”.
Surface reflectance Landsat 8 & 9 images were acquired for each of these training locations/dates via Google Earth Engine (GEE). Where multiple Landsat images overlapped within a 1-hour window for a single glacier (i.e. successive Landsat rows), images were merged using a median pixel value, as described by Aberle et al. (2025). For each training image five spectral indices were calculated to aid in image classification: Normalized Difference Glacier Index (NDGI), Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Normalized SWIR Difference Soil-moisture (NSDS) (Equations 1 to 5). Each of these indices was tested individually and in combination with the other bands/indices and was found to aid separation of one or more of the landcover classes of interest. Surface reflectance, surface temperature, and all 5 spectral indices data were extracted from pixel data at each of the labeled training data points (Figures 2 & 3).
\[
  NDGI = \frac{green - red}{green + red}
\tag{1}\]
\[
  NDSI = \frac{green - SWIR_1}{green + SWIR_1}
\tag{2}\]
\[
  NDVI = \frac{NIR - red}{NIR + red}
\tag{3}\]
\[
  NDWI = \frac{green - NIR}{green + NIR}
\tag{4}\]
\[
  NSDS = \frac{SWIR_1 - SWIR_2}{SWIR_1 + SWIR_2}
\tag{5}\]






Figure 2: The spectral fingerprint of surface reflectance and surface temperature for Landsat 8/9 images across 6 surface cover classes “cloud”, “ice/firn”, “rock”, “shadowed snow”, “snow”, and “water”. Band labels correspond to Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 (surface reflectance) data product naming conventions and represent “arosol”, “blue”, “green”, “red”, “NIR”, “SWIR1”, “SWIR2”, and “thermal IR” respectively.









Figure 3: The spectral fingerprint of five calculated indices, Normalized Difference Glacier Index (NDGI), Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Normalized SWIR Difference Soil-moisture (NSDS) from Landsat 8/9 images across 6 surface cover classes “cloud”, “ice/firn”, “rock”, “shadowed snow”, “snow”, and “water”.



For model training and testing a K-folds repeated cross-validation method was utilized with 10 folds, 10 repeats, and a partition (p) = 0.9 resulting in a 90/10 training/testing split, where all labeled data points are utilized in testing for exactly 1 of 10 folds/repeats. Using this training/testing framework a total of 129 distinct ML models were tested, across 10 model types, using a hyper-parameter grid search performed in R utilizing the caret package (Kuhn 2008). Based on the accuracy results of this training/testing model optimization process, the three best performing models were selected for additional model validation using previously unseen, spatially-temporally distant validation data. The top three, best performing models were, random forest, support vector machine (SVM) using a radial kernel, and SVM with a linear kernel Table 1.

Due to the spatial autocorrelation of the training/testing data, K-folds methods are prone to over-inflating model accuracy with geospatial datasets. Therefore, it is best practice to validate spatial ML models using an additional dataset which is spatially-temporally distant from the training/testing data, and which has never been seen by the model. In our study, we labeled 5,750 Greenland-specific validation points for 5 locations, across 8 Landsat images. These locations were chosen for validation to capture a range of regional variability across the island. The five validation locations are, Mittivakkat glacier (3 dates/images; south east), north west peninsula (2), south east island (1; southern tip), Freya glacier (1; north east), and north (1; Figure 4).






Figure 4: Locations of training/testing and validation datasets across Greenland, with labeled regions. For locations with both training and validation data the validation data was 39 months (3.2 years) temporally distant from the training data, on average. World Glacier Monitoring Service Benchmark Glaciers Mittivakkat and Freya labeled.



The three best performing ML models were retrained using 100% of the available training data (10,812 labeled points) and were further validated on previously unseen data. The overall accuracy of all models decreased between 1-8% from their prior K-folds accuracy but maintained a satisfactory ovrall accuracy. The best performing model on the validation data was the SVM linear model, with an overall accuracy of 93% (Figure 5). The F1 statistic (a measure of model performance) was 94% for snow and 91% for ice, the two most critical classes for accurate Accumulation Area Ratio (AAR) calculation.






Figure 5: Glacier surface classification confusion matrix for the validated surface vector machine learner with linerar kernel across 6 surface cover classes, normalized as a frcation of total validation points, color coded by accuracy.





1.2 Land Cover Classification

1.2.1 Data Acquisition
Following model validation, all applicable Landsat 8 & 9 Collection 2 Level-2, Tier 1 surface reflectance Science Products images from 2015-2025 during the ablation season (JJAS) which contained at least one peripheral glacier were downloaded using either GEE geedim python package or the United States Geological Survey (USGS) EarthExplorer data portal. Images taken on ascending orbits, and images which only covered the Greenland ice sheet but did not contain any peripheral glaciers were excluded. In total, 20,562 unique images were downloaded (~17 TB).


1.2.2 Image Preprocessing and Classification
Landsat images and the pretrained SVM model were uploaded to the Arizona State University (ASU) Sol supercomputer (Sol) for processing (Jennewein et al. 2023). Raw Landsat images were initially converted to surface reflectance and surface temperature data using established scaling factors for the Operational Land Imager (OLI) and Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) instruments respectively. Images were then masked to peripheral glaciers using a buffered version of the Randolf Glacier Inventory (RGI) glacier outlines (RGI Consortium 2023). A secondary cloud mask was applied based on a modified version of the Antarctic cloud mask developed by Moussavi et al. (2020). After masking, the five indices were calculated as with the training dataset.
Preprocessed images were classified according to the pretrained SVM (linear) model. For each classified image, glaciers with at least 70% classification coverage were identified from the RGI data, by a spatial query with the classified image. For each of the glaciers identified the surface area for each landcover class was extracted from the classified image along with relevant image metadata using the R sf package (Pebesma 2018). For each glacier observation the transient AAR was calculated according to equations 6 to 8. Each glacier observation and associated calculations was appended to a data file, culminating in ~4.6 million glacier observations. This data file was downloaded for further post-processing.
\[
Total\:Snow\:Area\:(km^2) = snow + shadowed\:snow
\tag{6}\] \[
Total\:Glacier\:Area\:(km^2) = Total\:Snow\:Area + ice/firn
\tag{7}\] \[
Transient\:AAR = \frac{Total\:Snow\:Area}{Total\:Glacier\:Area}
\tag{8}\]



1.3 Postprocessing
Glacier observation data was postprocessed in R using the data.table package for fast, efficient handling of large datasets (R Core Team 2021; Barrett et al. 2026). Spatial data was handled using the sf package (Pebesma 2018).

1.3.1 Quality Control and Data Filtering
A variety of quality control and filtering steps were utilized to ensure that appropriate annual (end-of-season) AAR values were identified from the transient AAR dataset. First, glacier observations were filtered by their calculated glacier area. Then they were filtered by cloud cover, shadowed snow ratio, glacier size, glacier slope, and finally by date.
The first observation filtering process leveraged the glacier area to identify and screen poorly classified images. The glacier area is calculated according to Equation 7, and the glacier area ratio is standardized by dividing the glacier area by its RGI glacier extent (circa 2000). Ideally, throughout the ablation season, the glacier area ratio is expected to vary smoothly from ~1 (spring; fully snow covered) to some minimum value (late summer; exposed ice and rock near terminous), followed by a rapid rebound (end of ablation; onset of seasonal snowfall). In practice a combination of cloudy images and poor image classification can drive the glacier area ratio down. To screen these poor-quality images a loess function was fit to the glacier area ratio data for each glacier-year. The residuals were calculated for each glacier observation, and observations with residuals < the 25th percentile per glacier-year were filtered out (Figure 6).






Figure 6: Graphical representation of the glacier area ratio, glacier observation filtering process for Mittivakkat glacier, 2024. A loess smoothing function (black line) is fit to the full dataset. Glacier observations with a model residual < the 25th percentile are removed (open red circles). All other datapoints are retained for further analysis (green points).



Several additional simple filters were applied to the transient AAR data according to AAR accuracy spot-checks and sensitivity analysis Table 2. After all other filters were applied, the number of remaining quality glacier observations were counted for each glacier year. Glacier years which did not have at least 9 quality observations were removed (see Section 1.4).

1.3.2 Annual AAR determination
From this filtered transient AAR dataset, the annual (end-of-season) AAR was identified as the minimum remaining transient AAR value. (Hereafter, AAR is synonymous with annual AAR, transient AAR and \(\overline{AAR}\) will be explicitly identified as appropriate.) After filtering 37,036 glacier-years had quality AAR data.


1.3.3 Mean AAR
The glacier-specific mean AAR (\(\overline{AAR}\)) was calculated as the arithmetic mean of AAR for glaciers which had at least 5 years of AAR data. In total, 3,679 glaciers had quality \(\overline{AAR}\) data.



1.4 Glacier-Year Observation Density Sensitivity Analysis
To quantify the number of quality images needed for accurate identification of the AAR, an observational density experiment was performed. Twenty-one well-observed glacier-years were identified, evenly distributed around Greenland, each with at least 30 quality glacier observations (post filtering). For each glacier a series of subseting experiments was performed where n randomly selected points were subset from the glacier-year data. Using the randomly subset data, the assessed AAR was selected from the artificially limited dataset and compared against the actual (known) AAR obtained from the full dataset. The n observations tested were 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, and each experiment was repeated 100 times, for a total of 18,900 simulations Figure 7. Based on the resultus of these simulations, at least 9 quality observations per year are needed to reliably identify the AAR Table 3.






Figure 7: Sensitivity of the AAR to the number of quality observations in the dataset. Observations are randomly subset from a selection of well observed glacier-years with at least 30 quality observations. Violin plots with jittered partially transparent points represent the density of the experimental AAR error relative to the known value.

1.5 Equilibrium AAR and Committed Area Loss
Equilibrium AAR (AAR0) values were estimated after Kern and László (2010). Disequalibrium (\(\alpha\)) and committed area loss (\(\Delta\)A) were calculated according to Box et al. (2022). The \(\Delta\)A values varried considerably by region, with the north (NO) and north east (NE) having the most committed area loss. However, the NO, north west (NW), and central west (CW) have the most committed area loss relative to their current glaciated extent, at 34%, 27% and 24% respectively. Furthermore, while the resulting \(\Delta\)A values are approximately centered on 0 (median = -0.3 km2) the distribution is not normal (Figure 8). Rather, the distribution is highly leptokurtic (kurtosis = 90.3), with a negative skew (skew = -5.2). This indicates that, while most glaciers contribute relatively little to Greenland’s cumulative committed retreat, a few large glaciers that are substantially out of balance with current climate conditions are contributing the majority of the projected area loss. Similarly, a relatively few large glaciers are dominating the \(\Delta\)A calculations on the positive side, particularly in the central east (CE).






Figure 8: The negatively skewed and highly leptokurtic distribution of committed area change.




1.5.1 Committed Area Loss Sensitivity Analysis
To further investigate the \(\Delta\)A results we conducted a sensitivity analysis for a range of plausible AAR0 values, from 0.5 to 0.8, for each region individually as well as for Greenland as a whole (Figure 9). While most regions exhibited relatively low sensitivity to AAR0 values, the NE and CE were both highly sensitive to a wide range of AAR0 values. Therefore, small differences in either \(\overline{AAR}\) or AAR0 in these two regions would result in relatively large changes to \(\Delta\)A.






Figure 9: Sensitivity of committed area loss to a range of plausible equilibrium AAR values. Thick lines color coded by region, thin black line for all Greenland. Steeper lines indicate greater sensitivity.





1.5.2 Review of Yang et al. AAR0 Estimates
An alternative and recently published approach to AAR0 estimates offered by Kern and László (2010) is the glacier-specific AAR0 values published by Yang et al. (2026). While the Yang et al. (2026) data is laudible, and one of the only glacier-specific AAR0 datasets available, it may not be well suited for use in Greenland. While we initially favored the Yang et al. (2026) estimates, the resultant \(\alpha\) and \(\Delta\)A calculations did not pass scruitany. The cumulative Greenland \(\Delta\)A utilizing the Yang et al. data was a positive glacier area change of ~3,000 km2, with many glaciers showing \(\alpha\) values > 1. Upon further investigation, we found that our \(\overline{AAR}\) classification and calculation methods were accurate, the \(\alpha\) > 1 calculations were largely being driven by implausably small AAR0 values. For example, consider this large glacier in the NW (RGI2000-v7.0-G-05-00250; Figure 10). This glacier is the most extreme example of a positive \(\Delta\)A in the dataset. With an \(\overline{AAR}\) of 0.63 and a realized area loss of < 2% from circa 2020 to 2025 this glacier appears to be relatively healthy. However, the Yang et al. (2026) data list the AAR0 for this glacier as 0.45, a shockingly low estimate. In fact, of the top 10 most positive \(\Delta\)A glaciers in our data (as calculated with the Yang et al. data), 7 of them have AAR0 values < 0.5 (the losest tested theoretical AAR0 value in our sensitivity analysis). Global paleio-climate AAR0 estimates are typically estimated as 0.58, therefore, values below 0.5 are quite low. Additionally, ice caps, as seen in our representative example, typically have larger AAR0 values, relative to equivalent mountain glaciers (Yang et al. 2026; Kern and László 2010).






Figure 10: Glacier RGI2000-v7.0-G-05-00250, 07/16/2022, located in the NW, part of a larger ice cap. \(\overline{AAR}\) = 0.63, AAR0 (Yang et al.) = 0.45, shown here at the end of the 2022 ablation season, AAR2022 = 0.45 (the lowest observed annual AAR in the dataset).



These results call into question the accuracy of the Yang et al. (2026) data within Greenland. Therefore, alternate AAR0 estimates were identified, and the Kern and László (2010) appeared to be a better fit for our study area. The updated \(\Delta\)A calculations using the Kern and László data shift cumulative Greenland committed area loss into negative teratory, matching well understood and widely observed global trends of glacial retreat, and \(\Delta\)A forecasts are roughly equivalent (equal order of magnitude) with actualized (observed) loss from 2000–2025. Overall, the Kern and László (2010) estimates provide much more defensible results of projected area change within Greenland, however, their AAR0 estimates only considered glaciers up to ~40 km2, ~7 times smaller than our largest glacier. Therefore, we present \(\Delta\)A values preliminaraly and caution against granular analysis of glacier-specific \(\Delta\)A.

title: Quantifying Climate Disequilibrium and Committed Retreat of Greenland’s Peripheral Glaciers Using Landsat-Derived Accumulation Area Ratios
